                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                    §                    OF TEXAS


                       COMMENTS OF INFINIUM OPERATIONS, LLC

                                       I.   INTRODUCTION

       Infinium Operations, LLC and certain of its affiliates (“Infinium”) develops, owns, and

operates eFuels plants that convert hydrogen and waste CO₂ into low-carbon transportation fuels.

Such facilities may qualify as large loads due the power requirements of their electrolysis and fuel

synthesis facilities. Today, Infinium owns one eFuels plant operating in Corpus Christi. It is

working with project investors to construct another eFuels plant in Pecos and is developing other

projects across the State of Texas.

       Infinium submits these comments in response to the latest memorandum in Project No.

58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards under PURA §37.0561,

particularly as it relates to large industrial loads in Texas. While Infinium supports the

Commission’s efforts to provide greater clarity and streamline the interconnection process, certain

proposed approaches may unintentionally disadvantage industrial developers by creating barriers

to investment and limiting continued project diversification across the state. Although data centers

and cryptocurrency facilities represent a significant and growing share of large load demand in

Texas, they are not the only contributors, and some proposed provisions may inadvertently favor

these participants—who are often better positioned to deploy large amounts of capital quickly—

over other industrial developers with different capital constraints and development timelines.
        We appreciate the Commission’s effort on this rulemaking and consideration of the key

issues we identify below.

                          II.   RESPONSE TO DISCUSSION DRAFT

Financial Security Requirements:

       Requiring developers to post large value collateral prior to completion of interconnection

studies continues to present significant challenges for appropriate project development staging,

particularly for large-load industrial and energy projects. While the reduction in the proposed

collateral requirement from $100,000/MW to $50,000/MW is a meaningful improvement, it still

represents a disproportionate burden at an early stage, when interconnection studies are intended

to serve as a screening-level assessment of site viability rather than a commitment to proceed to

construction.

       In early-stage development, well before a project reaches Final Investment Decision

(“FID”), developers typically do not have full financing in place. Instead, they rely on limited

early-stage capital to advance permitting, engineering, environmental work, and—critically—to

obtain a clear understanding of interconnection feasibility, cost, and schedule. For large loads,

this interconnection visibility is one of the most important inputs to determining whether a

project should advance at all. Requiring significant collateral before this information is known

forces developers to commit scarce capital without the foundational data needed to justify that

investment. Collateral is among the most difficult forms of early-stage capital to raise, as it offers

no return, carries substantial risk, and may remain tied up for extended periods without certainty

that the project will meet investment thresholds.
        This structure also creates an uneven playing field. Large data center developers and

similarly capitalized entities are often better positioned to absorb or deploy significant upfront

collateral, whereas smaller industrial developers face materially greater constraints. As a result,

these requirements may inadvertently favor a narrow subset of market participants, limiting

broader industrial development and diversification across ERCOT.

       Intermediate Agreement Phase Security: At the stage where interconnection studies

are being conducted, collateral should be structured to reflect the screening-level nature of the

process. Financial security at this phase should (i) be set at a modest level sufficient to

demonstrate project seriousness, and (ii) be fully refundable, less only reasonable and well-

defined administrative fees should a project not proceed to Interconnection Agreement Phase.

This ensures developers are not penalized for responsibly exiting projects that, based on study

results, are no longer viable, and provides a clear off-ramp for projects to be removed from the

queue—thereby improving overall queue efficiency. Greater clarity is needed in the proposed

rules on how such collateral will be used and administered.

       Interconnection Agreement Phase Security: Once a project elects to proceed beyond

the study phase and executes an interconnection agreement, financial requirements can

appropriately increase to reflect a higher level of commitment. However, it is critical that (i) any

collateral posted during the intermediate phase is credited or rolled forward into the

interconnection agreement requirements, (ii) the purpose and application of all financial security

is clearly defined and tied to identifiable costs (e.g., system upgrades, CIAC, or other project-

specific obligations), and (iii) such collateral not function as a duplicative or non-purpose-driven

fee layered on top of existing interconnection and upgrade costs. As currently drafted, there is
 ambiguity as to whether interconnection agreement collateral is additive to, or inclusive of, other

required payments, which creates uncertainty for developers and investors.

       Providing clear differentiation between these two phases—screening versus

commitment—and aligning collateral requirements accordingly will better support project

development, reduce unnecessary capital burdens, and maintain discipline in the interconnection

process without discouraging viable projects from advancing.




Interconnection Agreement Execution:

       The proposal to require execution of an interconnection agreement within thirty (30) days

following completion of the interconnection study is generally reasonable with respect to

demonstrating a developer’s intent to proceed. A 30-day window to make a go/no-go decision

based on study results is challenging, but workable. However, the requirement to simultaneously

execute the interconnection agreement and post all associated financial security and CIAC within

that same timeframe presents significant practical challenges.

       At the point of study completion, developers are only then receiving definitive

information regarding interconnection costs, required system upgrades, and associated timelines.

These inputs directly inform the sizing of financial security and CIAC obligations. Coordinating

the necessary financing—particularly for large-load industrial projects—requires engagement

with lenders, credit providers, and internal investment committees, all of which take time to

underwrite and approve commitments based on newly available study results.

       Establishing instruments such as Letters of Credit can be a time-intensive process, often

requiring 60–90 days (or more) to complete due to bank underwriting, know-your-customer
 (KYC) requirements, documentation, and internal approvals. Requiring these instruments to be

fully executed within 30 days of study completion is likely to create a bottleneck that delays

otherwise viable projects. These are also the most practical option of financial security for many

industrial developers.

       This structure also risks disproportionately favoring large, well-capitalized data center

developers that can deploy balance sheet capital quickly, while placing smaller industrial

developers at a disadvantage, as they must coordinate financing with external investors and

capital providers.

       To address these challenges while still maintaining discipline and commitment in the

process, one recommendation is that the Commission retain the 30-day requirement for

execution of the interconnection agreement but allow an additional period—such as sixty (60)

days following execution—for developers to post required financial security and pay CIAC. This

approach preserves a clear commitment milestone while providing a realistic window to finalize

financing arrangements based on known project costs.

       An additional approach the Commission could consider is utilizing the non-refundable

interconnection fee as a form of interim financial security at the time of interconnection

agreement execution. Under this structure, the interconnection fee would effectively serve as a

commitment deposit: if the developer proceeds to post the required CIAC and financial security

within the allowed grace period, the interconnection fee would be refunded or credited toward

project costs. However, if the developer executes the interconnection agreement and

subsequently fails to post the required financial security and CIAC within the specified

timeframe, the interconnection fee would be retained as a penalty for failing to proceed after

indicating intent to move forward. This approach provides a clear and immediate signal of
 financial commitment while avoiding the need to fully secure complex financing instruments

within an impractically short timeframe and helps address the challenges noted above regarding

financial security requirements that lack clearly defined uses, which can be difficult for investors

to underwrite and support.




Other Requirements:

       It is reasonable for the Commission to require site-specific studies and engineering

analyses, planning related to state and local regulatory approvals, backup generating facilities

information, and information pertaining to how the facility plans to procure power; however,

clear guidance on how such information will be used in the screening and approval of large loads

is critical. A key challenge under the existing interconnection framework has been inconsistency

among Transmission and Distribution Service Providers (TDSPs) in the type of information

required, how that information is evaluated, and the processes for study and agreement

execution. Establishing requirements without clear standards for their application risks

perpetuating—or exacerbating—these inconsistencies, leading to differing interpretations by

TDSPs and resulting in inequitable treatment of projects across the ERCOT region.

   Additionally, when considered alongside proposed financial security requirements and

obligations tied to meeting energization timelines, these information requirements may impose

an added burden on all parties without a clear nexus to how the information informs decision-

making within the interconnection process. Absent such linkage, there is a risk that these

requirements function primarily as administrative hurdles rather than tools that improve

efficiency, transparency, or reliability outcomes.
                                     III.   CONCLUSION

       We appreciate Commission staff’s consideration of these issues and look forward to

collaborating on this rulemaking.

                                                Respectfully submitted,

                                                  X             signature
                                                Liz Myers
                                                SVP, Strategy & Solutions
                                                Infinium Operations, LLC

             EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF INFINIUM OPERATIONS, LLC

 ● Infinium supports efforts to streamline large load interconnection rules but warns that

    certain proposals may disadvantage industrial developers and reduce project diversity by

    favoring well-capitalized data center and crypto operators.

 ● While reducing collateral from $100k/MW to $50k/MW is an improvement, requiring

    significant upfront collateral before interconnection studies are complete places

    disproportionate risk on projects at an early stage and diverts critical development capital

    away from meaningful project development activities.

 ● Collateral during the intermediate (study) phase should be modest and refundable (less

    admin costs), while interconnection agreement phase requirements can be higher but must

    be clearly defined, non-duplicative, and tied to actual costs (e.g., CIAC, upgrades).

 ● A 30-day window to execute an interconnection agreement is workable, but posting full

    financial security and CIAC in that timeframe is not; a 60-day post-execution window or

    use of the interconnection fee as interim security is recommended to better align with real

    financing timelines.

 ● Additional study, permitting, and operational information requirements are reasonable, but

    lack of clarity in how they are used—combined with inconsistent TDSP implementation—

    risks creating unnecessary administrative burdens and inequitable treatment across

    ERCOT.
